query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at.% aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that significantly improves oxygen resistance at extreme temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy that, in its baseline composition, exhibits rapid oxidation and the formation of thick, nonprotective oxide scales when exposed to extreme temperatures (≈1100°C) in air.
generation.intervention: A targeted minor compositional change: the addition of approximately 5 at.% aluminum into the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1100°C in a 21% oxygen atmosphere (air) continuously for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, continuous alumina (Al2O3) barrier on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form a thermodynamically stable and slow-growing alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier, reducing the ingress of oxygen and thereby mitigating further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-enhanced alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate—characterized by lower mass gain per unit area and a thinner, continuous oxide scale (approximately a 30–50% improvement) compared with the untreated alloy—while retaining its structural integrity.
generation.baseline: In its untreated state, the refractory high-entropy alloy rapidly forms thick, nonprotective oxides under 1100°C air exposure for 100 hours, leading to severe oxidation-induced degradation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable for refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature structural applications. Variations in processing history, microstructural features, or interactions with other alloying elements may influence the effectiveness of the alumina layer formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in oxidation resistance may vary with alloy processing conditions and the uniformity of alumina scale formation; potential interactions with other constituent elements may also affect the barrier properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the refractory high-entropy alloy from identical feedstock and processing routes: one with the standard composition and the other with an additional ~5 at.% aluminum. Subject both sets of samples to an isothermal oxidation test at 1100°C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) to quantify oxidation kinetics
Surface and cross-sectional imaging via SEM/EDS to assess oxide scale thickness and continuity
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis to confirm the formation of an alumina (Al2O3) scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified samples do not exhibit at least a ~30% reduction in mass gain and oxide scale thickness, or if XRD/SEM/EDS fails to confirm the formation of a continuous alumina layer compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

frame.limitation: The current alloy formulation lacks a robust, self-healing oxidation barrier under high-temperature conditions in oxidizing atmospheres.

decision.trend: Early investigations in refractory high‐entropy alloys have predominantly explored compositional adjustments (for example, by varying Cr content) and associated processing techniques (e.g., laser cladding) to moderate oxidation behavior. These studies showed that while modifications can refine microstructures and slow oxidation rates, they generally led to the formation of nonprotective or mixed oxide scales rather than a continuous, self-healing barrier. The body of work has incrementally tuned alloy chemistry with the goal of influencing oxidation kinetics, yet the formation of a fully protective oxide layer under extreme, prolonged high‐temperature conditions remains unachieved.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved challenge is to establish a robust, self-healing oxidation barrier that significantly improves high‐temperature oxygen resistance (e.g., at ~1100°C in air for 100 hours) without compromising the inherent structural integrity of the refractory high‐entropy alloy.
decision.lever: a targeted minor addition of aluminum (approximately 5 at.%) to the alloy composition
decision.why: Adding Al is expected to promote the in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing, protective alumina (Al2O3) layer, a mechanism well supported by prior work on oxidation resistance in high-temperature environments. This single compositional tweak directly addresses the gap identified in previous studies by leveraging the known barrier properties of alumina without necessitating extensive changes in synthesis or processing.
